gen-dafont-edo-sz-gf-noto-sans-old-turki: Cast-iron stature, one constant stroke: that's Edo SZ. Noto Sans Old Turkic is the plain sans, chunky and tall in the lowercase, its open-mouthed curves staying clear instead of clogging.
gen-dafont-edo-sz-gf-noto-sans-osage: Round and unfussy, Edo SZ gives its letters rims that match the stems, like cast iron. Noto Sans Osage fills the line with inflated bowls, and Edo SZ earns its keep big and brief.
gen-dafont-edo-sz-gf-noto-sans-palmyrene: Stout as cast iron, Edo SZ lets its lowercase stand without any swelling. It makes a loud display line, while Noto Sans Palmyrene is the quiet worker, with compressed ascenders and curves that stop short.
gen-dafont-edo-sz-gf-noto-sans-rejang: Steel-cable outlines and cast-iron stature: that is Edo SZ in lowercase. It is built for display, with no thick-thin shift, while Noto Sans Rejang does the reading work through wide, porthole-like counters.
gen-dafont-edo-sz-gf-noto-sans-sharada: Noto Sans Sharada reads bulky and clean, with open c forms that never close into rings. Edo SZ's tubular, wire-like letters give that body text a sturdy display partner.
gen-dafont-edo-sz-gf-noto-sans-tagalog: Classic in stature, Edo SZ gives display lines a cast-iron lowercase without any hairline-to-stem shift. Noto Sans Tagalog, meanwhile, fills the middle zone of the line and keeps generous gaps in its curves.
gen-dafont-eight-bit-dragon-gf-noto-sans: A relaxed stride across widely spaced, towering letters, that's Eight Bit Dragon, with a small, steady stroke difference. Noto Sans Adlam backs it up, curve endings kept well apart.
Noto Sans Imperial Aramaic points its c ends apart like pincers, with a short step up to capitals. And Eight Bit Dragon adds a gentle stroke modulation that keeps paragraphs comfortable to follow.
Eight Bit Dragon strides wide, its letters spaced far apart and towering. Noto Sans JP sweeps its curves open and stands on a very tall x-height, which matches that towering stature.
